summary: The FEC Framework needs configuration information to operate. This informational RFC describes how signaling protocols such as SAP, SIP and RTSP can communicate it between senders and receivers.

eli5.summary: Before using spare puzzle pieces, both sides need to agree on how. This tells how to share those settings.

questions: how to signal fec framework configuration
how does sdp carry fec configuration
subtitle: Using existing protocols to share FEC protection settings between senders and receivers.

tldr.problem: Forward Error Correction (FEC) requires configuration information to be available at both the sender and all receivers, but configuring each device manually is error-prone and does not scale.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC shows how to use existing signaling protocols—SAP for multicast and SIP or RTSP for unicast—to dynamically communicate FEC configuration information between endpoints.
tldr.outcome: The approach lets FEC protection be deployed without static manual configuration, using protocols already in place for multimedia applications.

today: RFC 6695 is an Informational RFC that describes how to communicate FEC configuration using existing signaling protocols. It has not been obsoleted and remains the reference for how the FEC Framework Configuration Information should be conveyed in multicast and unicast scenarios.

sections.title: Introduction and Context
sections.content:
The Forward Error Correction (FEC) Framework (RFC 6363) enables applications to protect media streams by adding repair packets that can recover lost data. To operate correctly, both the sender and all receivers must agree on key details: which flows are being protected, which repair flows to use, which FEC scheme to apply, and other parameters specific to the FEC scheme in use.

Normally, an administrator would manually configure these settings on each device. However, this does not scale when content is broadcast to many receivers (multicast) or when the number and identity of receivers changes dynamically (unicast on-demand). This document describes methods to communicate FEC configuration information dynamically using signaling protocols that multimedia applications already use.
sections.eli5: Before video streaming can use extra data to fix broken packets, the sender and receiver need to agree on how to do it. Instead of typing settings into every device, this tells how to send those settings automatically using video protocols.

sections.title: FEC Framework Configuration Information
sections.content:
Every FEC Framework instance needs to communicate five pieces of configuration information: (1) which flows are being protected (source flows), (2) which repair flows carry the recovery data, (3) which FEC scheme is used, (4) the size of source FEC Payload IDs, and (5) FEC-Scheme-Specific Information (FSSI), an opaque container for scheme-specific settings like buffer size and decoding wait time.

This information may be encoded in any format suitable for the signaling protocol—the RFC uses Session Description Protocol (SDP) extensively as an example, but XML or other formats are allowed. The key requirement is that the signaling protocol must know which encoding format is being used so it can parse the configuration correctly.

The RFC does not mandate how the configuration is encoded; instead, it explains that once a particular FEC Framework instance selects an encoding format, that single format is used for all its configuration information.
sections.eli5: The settings package needs five pieces: which data to protect, which extra data fixes it, what math to use, the ID size, and scheme-specific tweaks. The sender can use any format to write these settings as long as the receiver knows which format was chosen.

sections.title: Multicast Signaling Using SAP
sections.content:
For broadcast and IPTV scenarios where one sender transmits to many receivers, Session Announcement Protocol (SAP) carries FEC configuration information. SAP is a lightweight announcement protocol that sends UDP packets to well-known multicast addresses and ports. The sender periodically announces available FEC Framework instances using SAP messages, placing the configuration information (encoded in SDP or another format) in the payload.

Receivers listen on the standard SAP multicast address and UDP port 9875. When a SAP announcement arrives, the receiver extracts the FEC configuration and provides it to the FEC Framework module. The sender must repeat SAP announcements periodically—the RFC recommends every 60 seconds by default—so receivers that join late will still receive the configuration. If the sender wants to change the configuration, it sends a new SAP announcement with a different message identifier and optionally sends a deletion message for the old announcement.
sections.eli5: In broadcast mode, the sender shouts the settings at regular times to a well-known address so anyone listening can hear it. When the settings change, the sender announces new ones and deletes the old ones.

sections.title: Unicast Signaling Using SIP and RTSP
sections.content:
For one-to-one scenarios such as Video on Demand (VoD), the RFC describes using existing unicast signaling protocols. SIP (Session Initiation Protocol) already supports an offer-answer model where one party offers options and the other answers with its choice. The FEC configuration can be encoded in SDP and included in SIP INVITE and response messages, allowing endpoints to negotiate which FEC protection to use.

RTSP (Real Time Streaming Protocol) provides another path: the RFC defines an option tag called 'FEC-protection-needed' that a client can include in the Require header of a SETUP request message. The server responds either with a 200 OK message that includes FEC options (the available FEC Framework instances), or with a 551 Option Not Supported message if it cannot provide FEC protection. The client can then send a new SETUP message specifying which FEC protection was selected.

The key advantage is that both protocols already carry the parameters needed for media sessions, so FEC configuration fits naturally into their existing message exchanges.
sections.eli5: When asking for one video on demand, the client offers to use FEC and the server answers which methods it supports, or both agree using SIP's built-in negotiation.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC recommends that SAP messages be authenticated using Pretty Good Privacy (PGP) authentication to verify that announcements come from an authorized source. This protects against forged FEC configuration information that could disrupt service.

No additional security considerations are introduced beyond those already present in the underlying protocols: SAP (RFC 2974), RTSP (RFC 2326), and SIP (RFC 3261). The FEC configuration information itself is typically not sensitive—it describes how to add protection, not cryptographic keys—so protecting the integrity of the configuration is more important than encrypting it.
sections.eli5: SAP announcements should be signed so receivers know the settings really came from the sender. The settings are not secret, but they should not be fake.
